title: Storms Could Slow Thanksgiving Travel
summary: Thanksgiving is one of the busiest travel weeks of the year, and this year the weather may make it trickier. Storms on both coasts could delay flights and car trips just as families head out for the holiday. More than 3,700 flights were delayed on Monday, and Chicago's O'Hare Airport had a ground stop, which means planes waited on the ground instead of taking off. Airlines are also still working through problems from recent computer failures. Delta, one of the biggest airlines, says its operations have resumed after an automated system went down, but delays from the outage are still rippling through the schedule. On the West Coast, a series of storms from the Pacific is expected to bring heavy rain and mountain snow. In the East, a separate storm forming over the Gulf of Mexico could bring rain, strong winds, and snow to parts of the region. Florida may see even more rain after nearly a week of downpours that already caused flooding there. The storms arrive at the worst possible moment for travelers. Millions of people fly or drive to see family for Thanksgiving, and even a small delay can turn into long lines at the airport. Airlines say they are working to get planes moving again, and weather experts are watching the storms closely. For now, the advice is simple: if your family is traveling this week, check your flight before you leave home, and pack a little extra patience.
why_it_matters: Millions of families travel for Thanksgiving, so storms and airline problems can turn a holiday trip into long waits and missed connections.

background_read: Thanksgiving is a holiday in the United States when many families travel to spend time together, so the days around it are some of the busiest travel days of the year.
Airlines run on tight schedules, so when a computer system fails or bad weather hits one busy airport, delays can spread to flights across the country.
Storms form over warm ocean water and can bring heavy rain, strong winds, and snow, and airports may hold planes on the ground until it is safe to fly.
